content.text: Why do electrons flow through circuits? What makes them move? The answer is potential difference—often called voltage. Just as water flows downhill due to a height difference, electrons flow through circuits due to a difference in electrical potential. Understanding potential difference is essential for analysing and designing electrical circuits.
Potential difference (V) is the energy transferred per unit charge. The formula is V = E/Q, where E is energy in joules and Q is charge in coulombs. It is measured in volts (V).
is the energy transferred per unit charge as charge flows between two points.
means one joule of energy is transferred per coulomb of charge:

| Source | Voltage |
|--------|--------|
| AA battery | 1.5 V |
| Car battery | 12 V |
| UK mains | 230 V |
| Lightning | 100+ million V |
Energy supplied per coulomb BY the power source
The 'push' that drives current around the circuit
Energy transferred per coulomb TO a component

A lamp transfers 60 J of energy when 5 C of charge passes through it. Calculate the potential difference across the lamp.
The p.d. across a resistor is 6 V. Calculate the energy transferred when 3 C of charge flows through it.
In a series circuit with a 12 V battery, the p.d. across the first lamp is 7 V. What is the p.d. across the second lamp?
A heater operates at 230 V. If 2 A of current flows for 5 minutes, how much energy is transferred?
Three resistors in series have p.d.s of 2 V, 5 V, and 8 V. What is the supply voltage?
Electricity is often compared to water flowing:

| Water System | Electrical Circuit |
|--------------|-------------------|
| Water | Charge (electrons) |
| Flow rate | Current |
| Pressure difference | Potential difference |
| Pump | Battery/power supply |
| Narrow pipe | Resistor |
The pump creates a pressure difference that pushes water around. Similarly, the battery creates a potential difference that pushes electrons around the circuit.
A voltmeter is always connected in parallel across a component. An ammeter is connected in series. Mixing these up is a common exam mistake.
(This will be explored further in the lesson on electrical power.)
Around any closed loop in a circuit:
Sum of EMFs = Sum of p.d.s
Conservation of energy in electrical form
Mains electricity in the UK has a potential difference of 230 V, meaning each coulomb of charge transfers 230 J of energy. This is why mains electricity is far more dangerous than a 1.5 V battery.
— Voltage is a difference between two points, like height difference. Current flows; voltage is measured across.
— Voltmeters go in parallel. Ammeters go in series.
— Only true if resistance stays constant. V, I, and R are related by Ohm's law.
— The battery supplies energy (EMF). Voltage is the energy per unit charge.
— The potential difference is 'dropped' across components as energy is transferred. Total p.d. dropped equals EMF supplied.
— Zero p.d. across something just means no energy is transferred there. Current might still flow.

Explain why a voltmeter must have very high resistance for accurate measurements.

Potential difference: energy transferred per unit charge,
EMF: energy supplied by the source per coulomb
In series: p.d.s add up to equal the EMF
In parallel: p.d. is the same across each branch
Voltmeter: measures p.d., connected in parallel, high resistance
Voltage is measured across components, not through them
-- In series, p.d.s add to equal the EMF. (calculation)
In a parallel circuit, the p.d. across each branch equals the supply voltage. (recall)

A voltmeter is connected in parallel with a component. If it had low resistance, a significant current would flow through it, diverting current from the component and altering the circuit. High resistance ensures negligible current flows through the voltmeter, so it measures the true p.d. without affecting the circuit.
